title: Positive cosine and sine operators
subtitle: G2 lecture 046000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: Think back to two lines meeting at an angle.
body: The cosine tells us how much of a unit vector along one line survives when we project it onto the other. The sine tells us how much is lost into the perpendicular direction. A finite-dimensional pair of subspaces can have several principal angles, one for each independent principal plane. But a list of angles requires choosing principal vectors, and in infinite dimensions there may be no complete list of them. Can we encode the same geometry without first choosing any vectors at all? Yes.

slides.title: Start with a single tilted line
body: Call its horizontal axis U. Call the line tilted counterclockwise by angle theta V. We assume theta lies between zero and ninety degrees. Project a horizontal unit vector onto V. Its projection has length cosine theta. The part perpendicular to V has length sine theta. Squaring the two lengths and adding them gives one, by the Pythagorean theorem. Now remember the two projection matrices from our cosine–sine decomposition. Projection onto U keeps the horizontal coordinate and discards the vertical one. Projection onto V has cosine squared in the upper left, sine squared in the lower right, and cosine times sine in the two off-diagonal positions.

slides.title: From a squared difference to the sine operator
body: Let P be the orthogonal projection onto U and Q the orthogonal projection onto V. We will assume the subspaces are closed, so their orthogonal projections exist. Call their difference D: P minus Q. Because each projection is self-adjoint, D is self-adjoint as well. Its square is therefore positive: taking the inner product of D squared x with x gives the squared norm of D x. We also need an upper bound. For two orthogonal projections, the norm of their difference is at most one. Here is a proof. Split x into its part in U and its part perpendicular to U.

slides.title: Construct the cosine from what remains
slides.lead: The sine operator squared is D squared.
body: If sine squared plus cosine squared is to equal the identity, the natural cosine squared is the identity minus D squared. This operator is positive, since D squared is at most the identity. Take its unique positive square root. Call that the ambient cosine operator. We have now constructed both pieces without choosing a basis. The sine is the positive square root of D squared. The cosine is the positive square root of the identity minus D squared. Their squares add to the identity by construction. Both are positive. And they commute, because both are obtained by applying functions to the same self-adjoint operator D squared.

slides.title: Why the operators respect both subspaces
slides.lead: There is a second identity hiding in the projection algebra.
body: Expand D squared. It equals P plus Q minus P Q minus Q P. Multiply that expression by P on the left. Then multiply it by P on the right. The results are the same, because P squared equals P. The same argument works with Q. So D squared commutes with P and Q. Functions of D squared, including its positive square roots, also commute with both projections. This has a geometric consequence: sine and cosine preserve U and its orthogonal complement, and they also preserve V and its orthogonal complement. Each can be studied in smaller blocks, even when P and Q themselves fail to commute.

slides.title: A second cosine, seen from U
slides.lead: Let us now look only at vectors inside U.
body: Take a vector x in U and project it onto V. Its squared projected length is the inner product of Q x with x. Because P x equals x, this is also the quadratic form of P Q P restricted to U. Thus P Q P on U records the squares of the projection lengths. In a principal direction making angle theta with V, it acts by cosine squared theta. Taking its positive square root on U produces a positive cosine operator intrinsic to U. The corresponding sine comes from the positive square root of P times the identity minus Q times P, restricted to U. These source-side operators are useful because their singular values are indexed by directions in U.

slides.title: Zero and right angles without guessing
slides.lead: The Halmos decomposition tells us exactly what the endpoint angles do.
body: On a direction common to U and V, P and Q agree, so D is zero. The sine operator is zero, and the cosine is the identity. That is angle zero. On a direction belonging to U but perpendicular to V, P acts as one and Q as zero. There D has magnitude one. The sine operator acts as one and cosine as zero. That is a right angle. The same happens for a target-only defect direction. On a direction perpendicular to both subspaces, P and Q again agree, so the ambient sine is zero and cosine is one.

slides.title: The actual angle operator
slides.lead: We can go one step further.
body: Since the positive sine operator has spectral values between zero and one, we may apply the arcsine function by functional calculus. The result is a self-adjoint angle operator whose spectrum lies between zero and a right angle. Applying sine to it recovers the sine operator. Applying cosine produces the positive cosine operator. So we have an exact operator analogue of saying theta is an angle, rather than merely a number whose sine we happen to know. The construction is especially valuable when there is no complete basis of principal-angle eigenvectors. Functional calculus still makes sense of sine, cosine, and arcsine on the operator as a whole.

slides.title: Reconstruction
slides.lead: There are three calculations worth doing before moving on.
body: First, write the two projection matrices for lines meeting at angle theta. Subtract them and square the result. Check that sine squared theta appears on both diagonal entries. Second, use only P squared equals P and Q squared equals Q to show that the square of P minus Q commutes with P and Q. Notice that the statement does not require P and Q to commute. Third, identify the sine and cosine actions on each of the four elementary Halmos pieces.
